entry.title: Rewriting the abstract of LLM-JEPA
entry.content:
What I changed and why

The original abstract buries its lede: four of its nine sentences are field-level framing (vision beats language, a rhetorical question, “a testimony of the challenge”) before the reader learns what the paper actually built, and the single most important idea — that you get a JEPA objective for a generative LLM by treating a (text, code) pair as two views of the same knowledge — never appears in the abstract at all. The result is also unquantified (“a significant margin”) when Figure 1 has clean numbers to offer. I rewrote it to open on the mechanism and the finding, fold the motivation into one sentence, kill the rhetorical question, add a concrete number, and fix the hedging (“Thus far, LLM-JEPA is able to outperform”) and the “overfiting” typo.

Before and after

Before Large Language Model (LLM) pretraining, finetuning, and evaluation rely on input-space reconstruction and generative capabilities. Yet, it has been observed in vision that embedding-space training objectives, e.g., with Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), are far superior to their input-space counterpart. That mismatch in how training is achieved between language and vision opens up a natural question: can language training methods learn a few tricks from the vision ones? The lack of JEPA-style LLM is a testimony of the challenge in designing such objectives for language. In this work, we propose a first step in that direction where we develop LLM-JEPA, a JEPA based solution for LLMs applicable both to finetuning and pretraining. Thus far, LLM-JEPA is able to outperform the standard LLM training objectives by a significant margin across models, all while being robust to overfiting. Those findings are observed across numerous datasets (NL-RX, GSM8K, Spider, RottenTomatoes) and various models from the Llama3, OpenELM, Gemma2 and Olmo families.
After Vision models learn far better representations when trained to predict in embedding space — as Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) do — than in input space, yet LLMs are still trained almost entirely by reconstructing tokens. We bring JEPA to language with LLM-JEPA, which adds an embedding-space prediction loss alongside the usual next-token objective: whenever a dataset gives two views of the same knowledge — e.g., a natural-language description and the regex or SQL it specifies — we train the model to predict one view's representation from the other. This keeps the LLM's generative ability intact while sharpening its representations. Across the Llama3, Gemma2, OpenELM, and Olmo families and four datasets (NL-RX, GSM8K, Spider, RottenTomatoes), LLM-JEPA beats standard finetuning by large margins — e.g., it lifts Llama3 on NL-RX-SYNTH from 37% to 52% accuracy — and resists overfitting, with encouraging early results for pretraining too. Code: github.com/rbalestr-lab/llm-jepa.

The general rule

Lead with the mechanism and the finding; demote the motivation to one sentence — and put a number in. An abstract reader is deciding whether to keep reading, so the first two sentences should tell them what you did, how it works, and roughly how much it helped. Framing about the state of the field is a toll you make the reader pay, not the product; pay it once and move on. And never pose a rhetorical question (“can language learn a few tricks from vision?”) when you can just state the answer you found.
entry.summary: The abstract spends five sentences clearing its throat before telling you what it did — here's a version that leads with the finding, the mechanism, and a number.

entry.title: Critique of When Forgetting is Not Catastrophic: On the Mechanics of Spurious Forgetting

link.title: Critique of When Forgetting is Not Catastrophic: On the Mechanics of Spurious Forgetting

entry.content:
Summary of the claims

The paper argues that the accuracy drop we call “forgetting” during finetuning is really two processes on different timescales, and that conflating them is the field’s mistake:

  1. A shared, reversible common shift: every old memory moves in the same direction in hidden space, toward the region of the new answers. This is hiding, not erasure. The facts still rank correctly within their own answer region, and the shift is withdrawn on its own once the new facts are actually learned, producing the striking collapse → recovery → erosion curve with no replay.
  2. A slow, irreversible fact-specific drift: each old memory moves in its own direction, with no restoring force, so it only accumulates. This is the real, catastrophic erosion.

The common shift needs three ingredients, each shown necessary: shared key structure (keys are k_i = √α·μ + √(1−α)·e_i, α > 0), new answers concentrated in one region of the vocabulary, and normalization. RMSNorm is the load-bearing and counterintuitive part: it both amplifies the collapse (rotating states toward the shift, shrinking their individual parts) and then supplies the restoring force that withdraws it, captured in a closed-form scalar ODE whose recovery is gated by learning of the new facts, not by step count. The practical payoff is an internals-light repair: subtract the top singular direction of each weight update, which restores the hidden facts in a real pretrained LM. Validated across three scales: a minimal associative-memory model, a controlled attention-only Transformer on synthetic biographies, and OLMo-2 1B on CounterFact / EntityQuestions.

Strengths

  • It is mechanistic and falsifiable, not descriptive. The two-term decomposition is backed by a clean causal test: subtract the common component of the logit change and the collapse disappears entirely; keep only the common component and you reproduce collapse-then-recovery. That is a real knife, not a correlation.
  • The three-ingredient ablation is complete (remove key-sharing, answer-concentration, or normalization and the phenomenon dies), so the theory is not over-claimed.
  • The repair is genuinely useful and genuinely tested. It works on a real LM, and it is explicitly not a training rewind: at matched new-fact accuracy the edited model recalls more old facts than the trained one. The removed direction holds only ~8-15% of the update norm but has 0.75-0.97 cosine with the common shift, which is a satisfying “small, well-localized cause” result.
  • It dissolves a confusing empirical object. The “stability gap” (sharp early drop, then return) and linear-probe “shallow forgetting” become one thing: the common-shift hiding. It also explains why replay helps the trough but cannot stop erosion, which matches its own replay ablation (trough 0.17 → 0.50, but final only 0.54 → 0.62).
  • Honest grounding in prior phenomenology (availability vs accessibility; spontaneous recovery) without overselling the analogy.

Weaknesses

  • Scope is narrow: factual recall, first-token accuracy, one real LM (OLMo-2 1B). The entire story is key-value lookup. Whether “hiding vs erasing” even has the same meaning for skills or multi-step reasoning is untested, and that is where most practical forgetting lives.
  • The headline self-healing is cleanest where it is least realistic. The authors concede the normalization-driven recovery is probably weaker on real data; the full collapse → recovery → erosion curve is crispest in the minimal model and under a schedule deliberately engineered to make it observable.
  • A theory/experiment gap it does not close. The theory is gradient-flow, where learning rate only rescales time, yet empirically the depth of collapse grows with LR. That is left unexplained rather than flagged as a limit of the model.
  • A confound in the key real-LM result. Synthetic individuals recover; real entities never do. The paper attributes this to “what the subject reveals about the answer,” but the two conditions differ in other ways too (entity distribution, answer overlap with pretraining), and there is no stimulus set that varies only that factor.
  • It does not connect its irreversible term to the plasticity-loss literature, where it clearly belongs. “Fact-specific drift with no restoring term” is, operationally, a loss of capacity, and there is a mature line studying exactly that: how one update reduces what the model can later learn. Reading this paper’s erosion as interference, rather than as plasticity loss, is a missed unification. Likewise, the whole story hinges on normalization and the geometry of the minimum, which is adjacent to the flat-vs-sharp-minima and weight-decay results, none of which are engaged (see Further reading).

How it could have been improved

  • Measure future learnability, not just past recall. If fact-specific drift is plasticity loss, show it with a plasticity probe: after the update, how fast can the model learn a fresh task? That would connect the erosion term to the unified learning-dynamics / data-attribution framework and turn a qualitative claim (“no restoring term”) into a measured capacity curve.
  • Vary the geometry the theory says matters. The model predicts no recovery without normalization and a central role for the curvature of the minimum. So test LayerNorm vs RMSNorm vs none on a real LM, and measure whether a flatter pretraining minimum (sharpness-aware pretraining, or no-LR-decay pretraining) changes the collapse depth and the erosion rate. The paper brushes against sharpness but never measures it.
  • Turn the generalization-recovery tradeoff into a usable frontier. The repair costs new-fact accuracy because the removed direction also carries the signal that helps generalization. Sweep how much of the top direction to remove against new-fact retention and report the Pareto curve, so a practitioner has a knob rather than a binary edit.
  • Disentangle the real-entity confound with a synthetic stimulus set where “subject reveals answer” is the only varied factor.
  • Scale the repair. OLMo-2 1B only. Given that the ability to self-edit/repair is reported as scale-emergent in adjacent work, showing the rank-one edit holds at 7B+ and across model families would materially strengthen the practical claim.

Verdict

Accept, with the scope caveat. The two-process decomposition is a real conceptual contribution and the causal interventions are convincing within factual recall. The direction is worth pursuing: the rank-one “un-hiding” edit is practically interesting for continual learning and, more pointedly, for safety, since it implies that behaviors “forgotten” during finetuning may be only hidden and recoverable by a weight edit. The two things that would move it from “nice mechanistic result” to “load-bearing”: generalizing past key-value recall, and connecting the irreversible drift term to the plasticity-loss literature so that erosion is measured as lost learning capacity, not just lost recall.

Further reading

The adjacent literature this paper should be read against (how training in one place changes what the model can do or learn elsewhere):

  • Learning Dynamics of Continual Learning: A Unified View of Data Attribution, Forgetting, and Plasticity Loss — the unification the erosion term belongs in: how learning one token changes another prediction, and how updates slowly reduce what the model can learn later.
  • Can Scale Save Us From Plasticity Loss in Large Language Models? — GPT-style models lose plasticity in multilingual continual learning, and larger models only delay the onset; directly relevant to the repair’s scale dependence.
  • Weight Decay Improves Language Model Plasticity — a base model that looks worse after pretraining can be better after finetuning; an optimizer lever the paper’s normalization story ignores.
  • Pre-training LLM without Learning Rate Decay Enhances Supervised Fine-Tuning and (How) Learning Rates Regulate Catastrophic Overtraining — LR decay gives sharper minima that adapt and retain worse; a prediction this paper could have tested against collapse depth.
  • Sharpness-Aware Pretraining Mitigates Catastrophic Forgetting — flatter pretraining minima forget less after post-training; the curvature axis missing from this analysis.
  • Replaying pre-training data improves fine-tuning and Early Data Exposure Improves Robustness to Subsequent Fine-Tuning — replay and data-order angles that complement the weight-edit repair, and the claim that how a capability is learned decides whether it survives later finetuning.
  • The Piggyback Hypothesis of Generalization — narrow finetuning spreading to unrelated prompts through chat-template tokens; a different “spurious” spreading mechanism worth contrasting with the common shift.
entry.summary: A sharp, well-controlled mechanistic result I would accept, but it stops at factual recall and never connects its irreversible "drift" term to the plasticity-loss literature where it belongs.

entry.title: Critique of LLM-JEPA: Better Representations or Better Regularization?

link.title: Critique of LLM-JEPA: Better Representations or Better Regularization?

entry.content:
Summary of the claims

LLM-JEPA combines next-token prediction with an additional training objective that predicts representations of related information. The authors claim that this approach improves performance, prevents overfitting, and encourages more structured internal representations without additional inference computation.

Strengths

  • Simplicity: The method requires no substantial architectural changes or additional inference computation.
  • Empirical diversity: The authors evaluate multiple model families, datasets, and training settings.
  • Beyond accuracy: The paper investigates the geometry of learned representations, attempting to explain the mechanism.
  • Computational efficiency: JEPA-loss dropout offers a practical way to reduce additional training costs.

Weaknesses

  1. Embedding alignment does not necessarily imply better representations. Smaller singular values of the difference between text and code embeddings do not necessarily indicate lower rank or better semantic structure. In the extreme case, representation collapse would minimize these differences while eliminating semantic distinctions.

  2. Semantic learning or regularization? Improved generalization and reduced overfitting may result from the addion to the objective acting as a regularizer. In my opinion, the paper does not really distinguish between these explanations.

  3. Fairness of comparisons. LLM-JEPA receives additional hyperparameter tuning compared to standard fine-tuning. Furthermore, alternative loss functions in Table 3 are evaluated using the same loss weight, despite potentially different gradient magnitudes.

  4. Limited generalizability. The strongest improvements are observed on tasks where the data already contains two related views, such as a text description and its corresponding code. However, for ordinary text, it is less clear how to create meaningful pairs. Therefore, it remains unclear whether LLM-JEPA would be equally effective for general language model pretraining.

How it could have been improved

  1. Measure embedding norms, effective rank, and variance to distinguish meaningful semantic alignment from partial representation collapse.

  2. Compare against independently tuned regularization methods and introduce shuffled pair controls to investigate whether meaningful pairing is essential.

  3. Independently tune competing objectives under comparable hyperparameter search budgets and report actual training costs.

  4. Evaluate different view construction strategies, such as paraphrases, summaries, and masked text, alongside larger scale pretraining experiments.

Verdict

Worth publishing? Yes, with reservations. The method is simple, practically relevant, and supported by promising empirical results. However, the evidence for improved performance is stronger than the evidence that improved semantic abstraction explains these gains.

Worth pursuing? Yes. Combining generative and representation learning objectives looks like a promising research direction. Future work should prioritize understanding whether the improvements arise from semantic alignment, regularization, or optimization effects, rather than simply demonstrating additional benchmark improvements.
entry.summary: Examining whether improved performance reflects better semantic representations or an additional regularization effect.

entry.title: Papers worth knowing this week
entry.content:
“BERT-JEPA: Reorganizing CLS Embeddings for Language-Invariant Semantics”

Taj Gillin, Adam Lalani, Kenneth Zhang, Marcel Mateos Salles, 2026.

This paper uses multilingual parallel documents to train a BERT language model and applies the JEPA objective to the CLS token embedding. The authors show demonstrate that this added objective helps create a more language-agnostic embedding, benificial for various downstream tasks.

“Learning from Recurrence: Internalizing Depth-Induced Preferences in Looped Language Models”

Hui Chen, Joshua Elsdon, Can Goksen, 2026.

This paper relates to our recent discussion on looped transformers and latent reasoning. The authors show that deep recurrence often redistributes the probability the model assigns across the same leading options; therefore, distilling later recurrences into earlier ones can provide a better learning signal.
entry.summary: More JEPAs in Language and looped transformer distiliation.

entry.title: The points that matter in LLM-JEPA

link.title: The points that matter in LLM-JEPA

entry.content:
Most readers will look at the abstract, Figure 1 and maybe the intro. Here is what I think they should leave with, where the paper says it, and what is missing.

The three points

1. JEPA is a new way of training, invented by Yann LeCun, where part of the training happens in the latent space. You encode your signal (here it is text and code), and try to predict the target embeddings one from the other. In LLM-JEPA this is added on top of the usual next-token loss (Eq. 2): the embedding of the Text, passed through a predictor, should match the embedding of the Code under cosine similarity, so the model keeps its generative abilities.

2. Their way of training allows for better results, and they show a few reasons for it. Their latent space has a nicer geometry, the top singular values are better and their t-SNE plots look nice. On NL-RX-SYNTH with Llama-3.2-1B, accuracy goes from 51.95% to 71.10% while the next-token loss stays the same (Figure 3), so the gain comes from the JEPA term. The singular values of Enc(Text) − Enc(Code) are orders of magnitude lower (Figure 3), and the Text and Code clusters line up in t-SNE (Figure 4).

3. JEPA is more efficient for the same compute. In the paper, efficiency shows up as more accuracy for the same compute: LLM-JEPA beats regular fine-tuning at equal PFLOPs, and dropping the JEPA loss on 50–75% of batches makes it even better (Figure 5, Table 6). It also keeps improving over 6 epochs while regular fine-tuning overfits (Figure 1, right). The price is about 2× compute per training step, because of one extra forward pass.

Suggestions

LLM-JEPA is still an LLM: it keeps next-token prediction and only adds the JEPA term, so the question is not “JEPA or LLMs” but when the extra term is worth 2× training compute. The paper’s answer is: when the data comes in natural pairs. The big gain (about +20 points) is on NL-RX, where Text and Code are two clean views of the same thing. Without such pairs the gains shrink to about 1 point (NQ-Open 20.1 → 21.6, HellaSwag 69.4 → 70.5, GSM8K on Qwen3-1.7B 44.3 → 45.0; Tables 4, 5), and a later audit of 22 JEPA-style losses (Representation Without Reward) found no gain beyond seed noise. Everything is also at 1–8B and mostly fine-tuning; pretraining is tested only on small datasets. The paper should say this up front: name paired-view tasks (text-to-code, text-to-SQL, issue-to-diff) as the use case, and leave “better LLM training in general” as an open question until it is tested at pretraining scale.
entry.summary: LLM-JEPA gets more accuracy for the same compute and a better organized latent space, but mostly on paired text-code data.

entry.title: Teach Llm Jepa 1pxl
entry.content:
title: “Representation Collapse: When a Perfect Loss Means Nothing Was Learned” description: Why predicting embeddings can lead to trivial solutions and how different learning methods deal with this problem. paper: llm-jepa task: teach by: [golombi] —

Why this matters

While reading LLM-JEPA, I came across an interesting problem with training models to predict embeddings rather than tokens.

In standard language modeling, the targets are given by the training data. When predicting embeddings, however, the targets themselves are representations learned by the model.

This made me wonder: what prevents the model from simply learning embeddings that are easy to predict, rather than embeddings that actually capture meaningful information?

This problem is known as representation collapse.

The idea

How can a model minimize its loss without learning anything useful?

Suppose we have two inputs that express the same idea:

  • x: “Return the square of a number.”
  • y: def square(x): return x * x

We have an encoder E that maps inputs to embeddings and a predictor P that tries to predict the embedding of y given the embedding of x.

Consider the following simplified loss function:

\[\mathcal{L} = \|P(E(x))-E(y)\|^2\]

We would hope that minimizing this loss encourages the encoder to capture the meaning shared by the two inputs.

However, there is a much simpler solution. Suppose the encoder learns to map every input to the same constant vector c:

\[E(x) = c \quad \text{for every } x\]

If the predictor also learns to output c, we get:

\[\mathcal{L} = \|c-c\|^2 = 0\]

The loss is zero, yet the embeddings contain no information about the inputs.

To illustrate this, consider the following toy example:

Input Non-collapsed embedding Collapsed embedding
Dog [1, 0, 0] [1, 1, 1]
Car [0, 1, 0] [1, 1, 1]
House [0, 0, 1] [1, 1, 1]

In the second case, given only the embedding, we have no way of knowing what the original input was.

Why isn’t this a problem in standard next-token prediction?

Consider two training examples:

  • “The capital of France is” → Paris
  • “The capital of Italy is” → Rome

If the model produces identical representations for both contexts, its prediction head will produce the same probability distribution over the vocabulary for both.

Since the correct next tokens are different, the model cannot predict both correctly with high confidence.

The important difference is that the model cannot change the target tokens. In embedding prediction, on the other hand, the model can potentially change both the prediction and the target to minimize the loss.

How do we prevent collapse?

There are several interesting approaches to this problem.

Contrastive learning (SimCLR)

Instead of only encouraging related inputs to have similar embeddings, we also encourage unrelated inputs to have different embeddings. Mapping everything to the same vector is therefore no longer a good solution.

Variance regularization (VICReg)

We explicitly encourage the embeddings of different samples in a batch to vary. If all embeddings are identical, their variance is zero, and the model is penalized for it.

Momentum target encoders (BYOL and I-JEPA)

We use a separate encoder to produce the target embeddings. Instead of updating this encoder directly through gradient descent, we update its weights gradually using a moving average of the main encoder’s weights.

This means that the model cannot directly change the target embeddings during a gradient update. Together with other design choices, this helps prevent collapse.

Combining objectives (LLM-JEPA)

Another approach is to combine embedding prediction with standard language modeling:

\[\mathcal{L}_{total} = \mathcal{L}_{LLM} + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{JEPA}\]

Even if collapsing the representations reduces the JEPA loss, the language modeling objective still encourages the model to preserve information needed for token prediction.

This does not guarantee that collapse cannot occur in particular parts of the model, but it provides an additional incentive to learn useful representations.

A quick question

Would replacing Euclidean distance with cosine distance solve the collapse problem?

Think about it before reading the answer.

The answer is no. If every input is mapped to the same nonzero vector, the cosine similarity between any two embeddings is 1, so their cosine distance is still zero.

What I find interesting about this problem is that it highlights something we should keep in mind when designing loss functions: it is not enough to show that the solution we want minimizes the loss. We should also ask what other solutions minimize it.

Learn more

  • SimCLR: An introduction to contrastive learning.
  • VICReg: Preventing collapse through variance and covariance regularization.
  • BYOL: Learning representations without negative samples.
  • I-JEPA: Applying joint embedding predictive architectures to images.

entry.title: Representation Collapse: When a Perfect Loss Means a Useless Model

link.title: Representation Collapse: When a Perfect Loss Means a Useless Model

entry.content:
Why this matters

While reading LLM-JEPA, I encountered a fundamental challenge in self-supervised learning: representation collapse.

JEPA learns by predicting representations in latent space rather than reconstructing the original input. However, if both the predicted and target representations are learned, what prevents the model from mapping every input to the same vector?

The idea

Representation collapse

Consider an encoder trained to minimize the distance between representations of two views of the same input:

\[\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{x,x'}\left[\|f_\theta(x)-f_\theta(x')\|_2^2\right]\]

Consider two possible solutions:

Input Meaningful representation Collapsed representation
Dog (0.9, 0.1) (1, 1)
Augmented dog (0.9, 0.1) (1, 1)
Cat (0.1, 0.9) (1, 1)
Augmented cat (0.1, 0.9) (1, 1)

Both solutions achieve zero loss, but only the first preserves meaningful information.

The second is called complete representation collapse. The model achieves the optimal loss without learning anything useful.

A more subtle phenomenon is dimensional collapse, where representations are not identical but occupy a low-dimensional subspace, leaving much of the embedding capacity unused.

How do different methods prevent collapse?

SimCLR: Negative examples

Contrastive learning brings representations of positive pairs closer while pushing negative pairs apart. Mapping every input to the same vector is therefore no longer optimal.

BYOL and I-JEPA: Architectural asymmetry

These methods use a target encoder whose parameters are updated through an exponential moving average of the online encoder:

\[\xi \leftarrow \tau\xi + (1-\tau)\theta\]

Combined with a predictor and stop-gradient mechanism, this asymmetry helps avoid collapse in practice, without requiring negative examples.

VICReg: Explicit regularization

VICReg combines three objectives:

  • Invariance: align representations of related inputs.
  • Variance: prevent embedding dimensions from becoming constant.
  • Covariance: reduce redundancy between dimensions.

For example, its simplified variance loss is:

\[\mathcal{L}_{var}=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\max(0,\gamma-\operatorname{Std}(Z_j))\]

Constant representations have zero variance and are therefore penalized.

How does LLM-JEPA address this?

LLM-JEPA combines the standard next-token prediction objective with a JEPA objective:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{LLM-JEPA}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{NTP}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\text{JEPA}}\]

While the JEPA objective encourages alignment between semantically related inputs, next-token prediction encourages the model to preserve information necessary for generation.

This provides a complementary learning signal that may help avoid collapse, although it does not theoretically guarantee non-collapsed sequence-level embeddings.

Takeaway: A low training loss does not necessarily indicate meaningful representations. When designing a learning objective, we must consider not only the solutions we want to encourage, but also the trivial solutions it allows.

Learn more

  • SimCLR (2020): Contrastive learning with negative examples.
  • BYOL (2020): Learning without negative examples.
  • VICReg (2022): Explicit anti-collapse regularization.
  • Understanding Dimensional Collapse (2022): Partial representation collapse.
  • I-JEPA (2023): Predictive learning in embedding space.
entry.summary: Understanding why learning in embedding space can lead to trivial solutions and how modern self-supervised learning methods prevent them.

entry.title: Rewriting the abstract of LLM-JEPA
entry.content:
What I changed and why

The original abstract was good overall and conveyed the main message clearly. I added a brief explanation of how JEPA predicts the embedding of one view from another, along with a concrete example from language: a natural-language description paired with its corresponding code. This helps readers who are unfamiliar with JEPA understand the proposed approach on a first read.

Before and after

Before

Large Language Model (LLM) pretraining, finetuning, and evaluation rely on input-space reconstruction and generative capabilities. Yet, it has been observed in vision that embedding-space training objectives, e.g., with Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), are far superior to their input-space counterpart. That mismatch in how training is achieved between language and vision opens up a natural question: can language training methods learn a few tricks from the vision ones? The lack of JEPA-style LLM is a testimony of the challenge in designing such objectives for language. In this work, we propose a first step in that direction where we develop LLM-JEPA, a JEPA based solution for LLMs applicable both to finetuning and pretraining. Thus far, LLM-JEPA is able to outperform the standard LLM training objectives by a significant margin across models, all while being robust to overfiting. Those findings are observed across numerous datasets (NL-RX, GSM8K, Spider, RottenTomatoes) and various models from the Llama3, OpenELM, Gemma2 and Olmo families.

After

Large language models (LLMs) are typically trained to predict the next token in a text sequence. In vision, training objectives defined in embedding space have outperformed input-space reconstruction in some settings. Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) use this approach by predicting the embedding of one view from another. We introduce LLM-JEPA, a training objective that applies this principle to LLM pretraining and fine-tuning using paired views such as a natural-language description and its corresponding code. Across experiments on NL-RX, GSM8K, Spider, and Rotten Tomatoes, LLM-JEPA outperforms standard training objectives across models from the Llama 3, OpenELM, Gemma 2, and OLMo families and shows robustness to overfitting.

The general rule

When an abstract borrows a method from another field, explain what the method does in one sentence and give a concrete example from the new setting.
entry.summary: One sentence that makes people want to click.

entry.title: Week 5 in one page: Spurious Forgetting

link.title: Week 5 in one page: Spurious Forgetting

entry.content:
About the paper

Finetune an LLM on new facts and it often seems to forget what it knew before. Previous work showed that some of this forgetting is spurious: the old knowledge is still in the model, just hidden, and can be recovered. This paper asks when and why that happens. It finds that recall of old facts can collapse, then come back on its own as training continues, before a slower, permanent erosion sets in. The authors identify three ingredients for the spurious part: old facts queried in similar ways, new answers concentrated in one part of the vocabulary, and a normalization layer.

Our posts:

✍️ Writing. Rewriting the abstract puts the paper’s main point first, that forgetting during finetuning is two processes and only one is permanent, and replaces unexplained jargon with plain language. A copyedit of Section 2 introduces the two settings and the experiment before the results, shows the evidence that the old knowledge is hidden, not erased, and ends with the questions the experiment raises.

🧠 Learning. To understand how a model can lose access to facts without erasing them, we first look at where facts are stored. The post summarizes work showing that a transformer’s feed-forward layers act like key-value memories: each neuron detects a pattern in the input and pushes the model toward certain next words, and the final prediction combines many such memories.

📊 Visualization. A better Figure 1 removes redundancy: since one finetuning scenario is a special case of the other, it keeps a single panel and cleans up the rest, labeling the lines directly and shading the pretraining phase as context. Two redesigns of Figure 3 then explain why old facts come back: a schematic of the three phases, with and without normalization, showing where old and new facts land and which are answered, and an interactive story in which a shared shortcut helps the model learn the new facts but hides the old ones, then becomes harmful, so training pulls it back and the old facts reappear without being retrained. Two redesigns of Figure 5 show the evidence that removing a single direction restores old facts: grouped bars make the size of the recovery easy to compare against a random-direction control, and a redesign with one panel per experiment draws ordinary finetuning and the edit side by side, and adds the cost of the edit on the new facts, which the original left out.

🔬 Research. A literature review places the paper where four lines of work meet, from catastrophic forgetting to recoverable forgetting, and points to the paper that coined “spurious forgetting” as the one to read first. Two posts follow the authors’ path, one on Palit and Schölkopf and one on all five authors, from interpretability, causality and the study of how models learn facts to this paper. Two critiques ask how far the results go: one on the toy model questions whether the simplified model and synthetic data match real LLMs, and the other on the OLMo results asks why OLMo recovered old facts in only one of two experiments and proposes a cleaner test. Three follow-ups propose experiments on semantic structure, abilities beyond facts, and preventing the shift through training order.

💻 Coding. A ten-seed reproduction of Figure 2 rebuilds the paper’s toy memory and shows that the more the facts share, the sharper the collapse of old facts, followed by recovery and erosion. A rerun of Figure 1 reproduces the paper’s two finetuning scenarios, then rewrites the new facts in a different phrasing and finds that the wording changes what gets forgotten, and that the paper’s explanation does not cover every case.

🔭 Scouting. The scouting posts look for recent work on the paper’s question: when is lost knowledge really gone? Five papers on forgetting during finetuning start from the paper that named spurious forgetting and cover why reinforcement learning forgets less, when replay is enough, and how pretraining length matters. Two posts find the same pattern of hidden, not erased knowledge elsewhere: facts removed by editing a model can still be read from inside it, and information supposedly removed by unlearning hides in intermediate layers. Two more look at ways to forget less, such as deleting a tiny fraction of weights, and at a trend where much of “training” turns out to be a single shift, which echoes the paper’s shared shift.

📣 Communication. An eight-post X thread explains spurious forgetting, its mechanism and the class’s experiments, and connects it to machine unlearning, with an earlier X post inviting discussion. A post on AIDA shows how to structure slide posts (attention, interest, desire, action), with a Canva template, and the slides were also posted on Instagram and TikTok.
entry.summary: Our focus points from a paper on when forgetting during finetuning is not catastrophic.
